source_text: Διὰ τούτων δὲ ὁδεύειν δοκεῖ τῷ Κέλσῳ ὁ λόγος ἐπὶ τὸ δεῖν πάντας ἀνθρώπους κατὰ τὰ πάτρια ζῆν, οὐκ ἂν μεμφθέντας ἐπὶ τούτῳ· Χριστιανοὺς δὲ τὰ πάτρια καταλι πόντας καὶ οὐχ ἕν τι τυγχάνοντας ἔθνος ὡς Ἰουδαῖοι ἐγκλήτως προστίθεσθαι τῇ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίᾳ. λεγέτω ουν ἡμῖν, πότερον καθηκόντως οἱ φιλοσοφοῦντες καὶ διδασκόμενοι μὴ δεισιδαιμονεῖν καταλείψουσι τὰ πάτρια, ὡς καὶ φαγεῖν τῶν ἀπηγορευμένων ἐν ταῖς πατρίσιν αὐτῶν, ἢ παρὰ τὸ καθῆκον τοῦτο πράξουσιν; εἰ μὲν γὰρ διὰ φιλοσοφίαν καὶ τὰ κατὰ δεισιδαιμονίας μαθήματα οὐ φυλάττοντες τὰ πάτρια καὶ φάγοιεν ἂν τῶν ἀπηγορευμένων αὐτοῖς ἐκ πατέρων, διὰ τί οὐχὶ καὶ Χριστιανοὶ, λόγου αἱροῦντος μὴ τευτάζειν περὶ τὰ ἀγάλματα καὶ τὰ ἱδρύματα ἢ καὶ περὶ τὰ δημιουργήματα τοῦ θεοῦ ἀλλ᾿ ὑπεραναβαίνειν καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν παριστάνειν τῷ δημιουργῷ, τὸ ἀνάλογον ποιοῦντες τοῖς φιλοσοφοῦσιν ἀνεγκλήτως τοῦτο πράττοιεν; εἰ δ᾿ ὑπὲρ τοῦ φυλάξαι τὴν προκειμένην ἑαυτῷ ὑπόθεσιν ὁ Κέλσος ἐρεῖ ἢ οἱ εὐδοκοῦντες τοῖς αὐτοῦ ὅτι καὶ φιλοσοφήσας τις τηρήσει τὰ πάτρια· ὥρα φιλοσόφους γελοιοτάτους φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν ἐν Αἰγυπτίοις γενέσθαι φυλαττομένους ἐμφαγεῖν κρομύου, ἵνα τὰ πάτρια τηρῶσιν, ἢ μορίων τινῶν τοῦ σώματος οἷον κεφαλῆς καὶ ὤμου, ἵνα μὴ παραβαίνωσι τὰ ὑπὸ πατέρων αὐτοῖς παραδοθέντα. καὶ οὔπω λέγω περὶ τῶν τὰς τοῦ σώματος φλυαρίας ἐν φύσαις φριττόντων τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ὅτι, ἐὰν ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων τις φιλοσοφήσῃ καὶ τηρήσῃ τὰ πάτρια, γελοῖος ἂν εἴη φιλόσοφος ἀφιλόσοφα πράττων. οὕτως οὖν καὶ ὁ ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου προσαχθεὶς ἐπὶ τὸ σέβειν τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν καὶ διὰ τὰ πάτρια κάτω που μένων παρὰ τοῖς ἀγάλμασι καὶ τοῖς ἀνθρωπίνοις ἱδρύμασι καὶ μὴ βουλόμενος ἀναβῆναι τῇ προαιρέσει πρὸς τὸν δημιουργὸν παραπλήσιος ἂν γένοιτο τοῖς μαθοῦσι μὲν τὰ φιλοσοφίας φοβουμένοις δὲ τὰ μὴ φοβερὰ καὶ νομίζουσιν ἀσέβειαν εἶναι τὸ τοιῶνδε ἐμφαγεῖν.
thought_title: Philosophers do not keep foolish ancestral customs
pass_a_gloss: Through these Celsus's argument (λόγος) seems to travel (ὁδεύειν) toward [the claim] that all men must (δεῖν) live according to ancestral things (τὰ πάτρια), not being blamed (μεμφθέντας) for this; but Christians, having abandoned (καταλιπόντας) ancestral things and not being some one nation (ἔθνος) as Jews, blameworthily (ἐγκλήτως) attach themselves (προστίθεσθαι) to the teaching (διδασκαλία) of Jesus. Let him tell us then whether (πότερον) those philosophising (φιλοσοφοῦντες) and being taught not to be superstitious (δεισιδαιμονεῖν) will fittingly (καθηκόντως) abandon ancestral things, so as even to eat of things forbidden (ἀπηγορευμένων) in their homelands (πατρίσιν), or will do this contrary to what is fitting (παρὰ τὸ καθῆκον)? For if because of philosophy and the teachings (μαθήματα) against superstitions (δεισιδαιμονίαι), not keeping (φυλάττοντες) ancestral things, they would even eat of things forbidden them from their fathers, why would not Christians also, reason (λόγος) requiring (αἱροῦντος) not to fuss about (τευτάζειν) statues (ἀγάλματα) and shrines/set-up images (ἱδρύματα) or even about the works/creations (δημιουργήματα) of God but to climb above (ὑπεραναβαίνειν) and present (παριστάνειν) the soul to the Creator (δημιουργός), doing what is analogous (τὸ ἀνάλογον) to the philosophers, do this blamelessly (ἀνεγκλήτως)? But if, for the sake of guarding the thesis (ὑπόθεσις) set before himself, Celsus or those well-pleased (εὐδοκοῦντες) with his views shall say that even one having philosophised will keep (τηρήσει) ancestral things, it is time (ὥρα) to say that philosophers, so to speak (φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν), become most ridiculous (γελοιοτάτους) among Egyptians, guarding against (φυλαττομένους) eating (ἐμφαγεῖν) an onion (κρόμυον), so that they may keep ancestral things, or certain parts (μόρια) of the body such as head and shoulder (ὦμος), so that they may not transgress (παραβαίνωσι) the things handed down (παραδοθέντα) to them by fathers. And I do not yet speak (οὔπω λέγω) of those of the Egyptians shuddering (φριττόντων) at the nonsense/trivial noises (φλυαρίας) of the body in breakings of wind (φύσαις), that if anyone from such philosophise and keep ancestral things, he would be a ridiculous philosopher doing unphilosophical things (ἀφιλόσοφα). So thus too the one brought (προσαχθείς) by reason (λόγος) to revere (σέβειν) the God of the whole (τῶν ὅλων θεός), and because of ancestral things remaining somewhere below (κάτω) beside the statues and human shrines (ἀνθρώπινα ἱδρύματα), and not wishing to go up (ἀναβῆναι) in his choice (προαίρεσις) to the Creator, would become like (παραπλήσιος) those who have learned the things of philosophy but fear (φοβουμένοις) the things not fearful and think it impiety (ἀσέβεια) to eat of such and such.

pass_b_english: By these words Celsus’s argument seems to be making its way to the claim that all men ought to live according to their ancestral customs, and would not be blamed for doing so, while the Christians, who have abandoned their ancestral customs and are not one particular nation, as the Jews are, are open to blame for attaching themselves to the teaching of Jesus.

Let him tell us, then: will those who study philosophy and are taught not to be superstitious be right to abandon their ancestral customs, so far as even to eat things forbidden in their homelands, or will they be doing what is not fitting? For if, because of philosophy and the lessons they learn against superstition, they do not keep their ancestral customs and would even eat what their fathers forbade them, why should Christians not do this without blame as well? For reason requires them not to busy themselves with statues and shrines, nor even with the works of God, but to rise above these and to present the soul to the Creator; in this they do what corresponds to what the philosophers do.

But suppose that Celsus, or those who approve of his views, will say, to protect the position he has set himself, that even a man who has taken up philosophy will keep his ancestral customs. Then it is high time for philosophers, among the Egyptians for instance, to become utterly ridiculous, taking care not to eat an onion, so as to keep their ancestral customs, or certain parts of the body, such as the head and the shoulder, so as not to break what their fathers handed down to them. And I am not yet speaking of those Egyptians who shudder at the trivial noises the body makes in passing wind, to point out that if one of these becomes a philosopher and keeps his ancestral customs, he would be a ridiculous philosopher doing unphilosophical things.

In the same way, then, a man who has been led by reason to worship the God of the universe, and who because of his ancestral customs stays somewhere down below among the statues and the shrines men have set up, and is unwilling to rise to the Creator by his own choice, would be like those who have learned the lessons of philosophy, yet fear what is not to be feared and think it impiety to eat this or that.
notes: The first paragraph is Origen's summary of where Celsus's argument tends, not a quotation, so no quotation marks. λόγου αἱροῦντος (paragraph 2) and ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου προσαχθείς (paragraph 4) are rendered 'reason'; Origen may intend a play on the divine Word as well, but the parallel with the philosophers points first to reason, so lower-case 'reason' is kept in both places. τευτάζειν: 'to be busy/fuss about'. ἱδρύματα: things set up, i.e. shrines and erected images. φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν taken as the idiom 'for instance', qualifying ἐν Αἰγυπτίοις (reviewer: the earlier 'it is time to say ... so to speak' rendered εἰπεῖν twice). The onion, head and shoulder: Egyptian food taboos; ἐμφαγεῖν governs both κρομύου and μορίων. τῶν τὰς τοῦ σώματος φλυαρίας ἐν φύσαις φριττόντων: those who shudder at the body's trifling noises in breaking wind (an Egyptian cult reported by later Christian writers); the translation keeps the sense without crudeness. Possible faint echo in 'present the soul to the Creator' of Romans 12:1 (παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα), not cited inline as the wording differs. No Scripture cited.
